Article:
Richmond, Oct. 1 - Within the last three days, we
understand that the dead body of a black man was floating
on the surface of the basin and was supposed to have risen
from its bottom, or that of the canal. It exhibited the
most suspicious signs of murder, the skull particularly
being very much battered and broken. It is said that the
deceased was a boatman from the upper country and that, in
an affray with another boatman, the deceased was knocked in
the head, dragged into the water and sunk. A coroner's
inquest called upon the body. It is said that the
principal, if not the only witness, is a deaf and dumb
woman, who made signs that she saw the murder at night and
then saw the body cast into the water. She is understood to
have made signs also that she will be able to recognize the
murderer. We understand that an order has been sent up to
Lynchburg for the purpose of apprehending the black man
suspected of the murder. The case of a murder being tried
on the evidence of a deaf and dumb person is perhaps a
singular one in the annals of jurisprudence. Who is to be
the interpreter in such a case? What rule is to be pursued?

An anti-slavery meeting was lately called in Boston, when
several thousand persons attended with the intention of
lynching Thompson and Garrison. The former did not make his
appearance, but they caught the latter, crouched under a
pile of boards in the second story of a carpenter's shop. A
rope was immediately fastened around his neck and arms, and
he was led into the streets, where the civil officers
arrested him and committed him to jail. He has since been
released and fed from the city. Thompson has gone to
Canada.

The New Bedford Mercury of Saturday, contains a statement
of the most horrid massacre of seventy native missionaries
at Wallis Island in the South Sea, in August, 1835. Mr.
William N.J. Barnard, formerly Second Officer on the ship
Selma, of New Bedford, who arrived there in the Parachute a
few days since, furnished the statement to the Mercury. It
appears from his journal that the English Missionaries at
Keppel Island, one of the Friendly group, conceived the
extraordinary plan of attempting to introduce Christianity
at Wallis Island, by sending native teachers and
missionaries, thinking they would meet with less opposition
than foreigners. They procured them passage to the island;
horrid to relate, soon after they landed, the whole number
were murdered in the most barbarous and inhumane manner.
Mr. Barnard was at the island at the time the massacre took
place, and left in the sloop of war Vincennes when she
touched at that place. He left the latter vessel at Cape
Town. Fanaticism and Outrage. Seldom have we heard a more

Lynch Law.- The Nashville Banner, of the 30th ult.,
contains a full report of a trial in the Circuit Court of
the United States for the District of West Tennessee, in
which Arson Moony was plaintiff, and Egbert Shepherd,
Joseph Jones, Jacob F. Harrington, and 10 others, citizens
of the State, were defendants. The transaction out of which
it grew took place on the 4th of September, 1835. The
plaintiff, it seems, had fallen under suspicion as a
kidnapper, or slave stealer, whereupon certain inhabitants
of Brownsville constituted themselves a Lynch Court, seized
the plaintiff in the dead of night, tried him, convicted
him, and then proceeded to punishment by inflicting one
hundred lashes with cowskin, branding him on the cheek with
the letter R, and commanding him to leave the country. The
trial was regularly conducted, defendants' witnesses being
subpoenaed and brought into court, some of them from a
distance of forty miles, at the expense of the now
defendants. It was very numerously attended by spectators
and assistants from all parts of the county. During the
progress of the trial, some merciful individuals among the
crowd suggested the expediency of hanging the now
plaintiff, but their advice was overruled by a solemn vote.
The jury in the Circuit Court gave a verdict of 1000
dollars and costs against five of the defendants.

Milledgeville, Nov. 16, 1837, A novel and interesting
incident occurred in the House of Representatives this
morning. One of the Bibb members presented a memorial from
Robert Beasley, stating that some few years ago he
purchased of a slave trader a negro woman and her sucking
child not doubting but that the woman was its mother.
Subsequent developments, however, had convinced him that an
imposition had been practiced upon him in the sale of the
child that instead of being born of a slave, it was the
offspring of a white woman from whom it had been stolen, or
who had abandoned it. The object of the memorial was, to
move the Legislature to change the name of the foundling
from that of William Gas (known in the bill of sale of the
slave trader) to that of William Crockett Beasley and to
restore to him the natural rights of which he had been
unjustly deprived. A thrill of admiration passed through
the House. Mr. Beasley was in the lobby and held up the
child in his arms a fairer, prettier, more intelligent
looking boy, need never be desired. Many an old bachelor's
mouth watered. The House went into committee of the whole,
had the child in the midst of them, and everyone we believe
was satisfied of his whiteness and his title to his
freedom. Macon Telegraph. Lynch Law - On Tuesday evening

The sun was setting with splendor and glow unequalled even
in the golden skies of fair Italia's land. Masses of cloud
assumed every possible variety of wondrous form and
gorgeous tint. Dark and mountainous appearances in the fore
part faded in the center to clear and sunlit distance.
Rocky slopes and castellated crags frowned over an
extensive valley of inconceivable loveliness and streams of
shining silver meandered through the purple and yellow
fields. It was a most remarkable combination of effect and
elicited general surprise and admiration. The whole of the
passengers collected on the after part of the upper deck,
and when the first expressions of delight had passed away,
they gazed in silence upon this striking development of the
beauties of nature. One of the passengers, a stout
farmer-looking man, with his wife and daughter hanging on
his arms, took off his hat, and said in a loud tone, 'These
are thy works, Parent of Good! The heavens declare thy
glory, Lord, and the firmament proclaims thy handiwork.
Blessed be the name of the Lord God.' These apostolic
quotations forcibly struck the minds of the standers-by,
and, with one accord, the hats of the male passengers were
removed from their heads. A holy feeling of reverential awe
pervaded our bosoms as we looked through nature up to
nature's God. A book from his pocket and in wanting tone
requested his brethren to assist him in improving the
occasion. He mounted the top of the rudder post, and gave
out two lines of hymn in a chanting drawling manner, and
led off the singing at the top of his voice. One or two of
his friends joined in the discord, but the rest put on
their hats, and turned jeeringly away. 'There,' said my
friend the Colonel, 'you may note the difference between
the effects of genuine impulsive piety and the second-hand
cant of the Pharisee the outward spiritual sign and the
inward spiritual grace. The righteous overmuch thrusts his
worldly sanctity down your throat in disagreeable doses but
the voice of pure religion emanates from the heart and is
sure to find a responsive chord.' Passing forward, I
overheard one of the deck hands thus deliver himself in
communion sweet with the freemen. 'Them there psalm singers
aboard boats is never no good. Went as hired help to two of
'em west of the mountains and down the Mississippi; they
were real stingy and mean they would pick pismire off the
ground, and steal the crumb out of his mouth. They used to
preach and pray, and sing all day, and steal niggers at
night. They got caught in Loosely and they were lynched
right away, and I guess, if I hadn't streaked, I should
have been lynched too, for keeping bad company.' The old
Colonel bade me farewell and, dreading the effects of the
night breeze on the lake, retired to his berth. The lights
of Cleveland, my port of destination soon appeared in view.
I selected my portmanteau from the general mass of luggage;
and, while inquiring for a porter, I saw a police officer
busily engaged in handcuffing the psalm singer. The
constable had been some time on the watch for his victim,
who was principal agent for the western gang of
counterfeiters.

Geneva Hail Storm.-Crop Destroyed. Tuesday afternoon last,
a heavy storm of hail and rain, accompanied by thunder,
lightning and wind, passed a little west of us, prostrating
in its path the crops of the farmer, the trees of the
forest, breaking down glass, blowing down chimneys, etc.
The fields that lay in its track are completely threshed
out, and most of them not worth harvesting. With us,
however, the whole passed off very quietly, with merely a
refreshing shower. At Geneva, seven miles west, much damage
was done to the buildings. Pieces of ice fell weighing an
ounce, and if reports can be relied upon, those weighing
much heavier. The track which this storm took made clean
work for the farmers.-Observer. Ominous: Saturday last,

Employment - There are a great many mechanics, laborers,

is in truth often used with great propriety-for we know
many worthy young men of capacity, intelligence, and
industrious habits, who have so long been doing nothing, or
filling mere temporary situations, that idleness has become
to them an intolerable burden. All they ask is employment,
till the dawning of better times. If those at the North who

wealth and greatness but those, who, from short-sighted
views, or from ignorance of the real state of affairs in
this quarter, effect nothing by coming to the South except
their own impoverishment. Far better were it for young men

to 'let well enough alone' than to emigrate under the vague

interest not only of the whole country, but of the owners
is for them to determine. Everything which alienates their
minds, then it would seem evident must go far to obstruct
the progress of emancipation. To excite prejudices, to
arouse pride, to provoke passion, is not, in ordinary
cases, thought to be the best mode of
persuasion.-Connecticut Observer. Melancholy Occurrence.-We

were drowned. The names of the lost were Mrs. Richardson,

the schooner, whose wife was one of the three ladies

Are these foreign hordes fit to share our liberties? This
question is one of fearful import and involves principles
and opinions that lie deep at the foundation of our
national permanency. We do not hesitate to say that they
are not fit, because they do not feel, as the natives of
the country, that strong inborn attachment that is so
essential to the greatness and prosperity of people. They
arrive in this country, without knowing one word of the
history of its rise and progress, and impressed with the

Attempt at Lynching. Vicksburg has been the scene of
another disorderly and illegal proceeding, which resulted
in bloodshed and death. The particulars are given at full
length in the Register of Saturday last; but we have room
merely for general notice of the affair. It seems that some
ten or fifteen persons, ardent lovers of justice and social
order, armed themselves with muskets, ropes, etc., and
proceeded, about 1 o'clock on Thursday night the 23rd ult.,
to inflict summary justice upon a family of four Germans,
named Flekenstein, (a father and three sons,) who lived in
the upper part of the town, and who, it was said, kept a
disorderly house. They demanded admission. This being
refused, they broke open the outer door and entered, J. A.
Helt, a German, and an unusually rash and adventurous young
fop, leading the way. Before he entered he called to his
comrades 'who will go in with me if I lead the way?'
Several replied that they would. The family was in the
upper story of the house. He commenced ascending the
stairs, when, perhaps dreading the resistance of some one
he saw, or more effectively to clear the way, he discharged
one of his pistols and wounded one of the sons of
Flekenstein severely in the neck and jaws. A volley of four
or five shots was almost instantly returned. Helt fell
dead, piece of the skull being torn off and almost the
whole of the brains dashed out. His comrades seeing him
fall, suddenly took to their heels and no more was seen of
them. Some other names have been communicated to us, but we
refrain from giving them at present, lest we should either
injure innocent individuals or prejudice the administration
of justice. It is thought that the wounds of Flekenstein
will not seriously endanger his life. An inquest was held
over the body of Helt, and verdict rendered that he 'came
to his death by the hands of one of the three
Flekensteins.' Measures have been taken to bring the
offenders to justice at the next term of the criminal
court.

and Manchester Railroad Bank against Dr. Riddell. The
defendants plead usury. On the trial, there was no evidence
to sustain other than that the Bank paid the proceeds of
the discounted note, on which the suit was instituted, in
its own notes during its suspension of specie payments,
which had since changed. The jury, after deliberating for
two days, returned a special verdict in favor of the
plaintiff for the amount the note and interest, payable in
the notes of the Benton and Manchester Railroad Bank, or
their equivalent. The informed the jury that the verdict
was not legal, nor was it in a form that would justify the
court. They must find a specific verdict for the plaintiff
or find generally for the defendant. He further instructed
them that the fact of the notes of the Bank devalued at the
time of the negotiation of the note was no evidence that
the Bank had taken usurious interest. They returned to
their room, and again appeared and informed the judge that
they could not agree on any other verdict. The counsel for
the Bank agreed to withdraw a juror, and make a mistrial,
and agreed to continue all of the Bank roles in consequence
of the excitement of the people against the Banks, which
seemed to have reached the jurors, under the hope and
expectation that the excitement would subside before the
next term. The judge sanctioned the continuation of the
cases and commented on the extraordinary and peculiar state
of things that existed in the country. He remarked he had
never before known a County jury to differ so widely on a
question of law, which seemed to have been brought about by
the members of the bar, some of whom were employed against
the Banks. Although he had no doubt of the honest
intentions and pure motives of the jurors, he remarked that
such an extraordinary state of things was calculated to
subvert the ends of justice. Some of the jury, as well as
the members of the bar, misconstrued the remarks of the
judge and presented him as having said that the conduct of
the jurors was calculated to subvert the ends of justice.
Much excitement was produced among the jurors and people in
the court yard. A member of the bar informed the judge that
the remarks had been misconstrued by the jurors. The judge
called the jurors and explained what he did say. The jurors
asked the judge whether he had not made use of the
offensive mentioned attributed to him. The judge answered
that he did not. Col. Alston, standing without the bar,
replied: you did say so, the judge ordered him to be fined
a hundred dollars for contempt of court. This explanation
did not seem to satisfy the populace, who were already
agitated on the Bank question, some under artificial
stimulants, and they became more clamorous and noisy and
collected in considerable numbers around and near the
court-house threatening the judge in bitter terms and
menacing him with personal violence. It was on Thursday
evening. When court adjourned, the judge left out at the
front door of the house on his way to his lodgings when he
was pursued by Col. Alston, who requested an interview. The
judge declined having conversation with him at that time.

Article:
Not long since a gambler had a game played upon him by the
deck hands and firemen on board one of our Western
steamers, a game even stronger than that played by Second
Municipality on this class of the community in New Orleans.
It seems that he had made out to strike up a small game of
poker with some of the deck hands, and that by dint of
cheating, putting up the cards, and other tricks known only
to those up to, and who make a living by, 'handing the
papers,' he had transferred nearly all the surplus revenue
from their pockets into his own. He scuffled and shuffled
to all appearances fair for some time, but was finally
caught at some trick, which at once led the honest
steamboatmen into the secret of how the thing was done and
proved that they lost their money by any other than the
'clean thing.' The game, as a matter of course, was blocked
at once, and demonstration immediately made that the
gambler should fork over his ill-gotten gains. This he
flatly refused to do; said that he had won the money fair,
and that he was very clear of parting with what he had come
honestly by. They still persisted, and he still refused.
The boat then stopped to wood, when the men, finding it
useless to attempt regaining their money by fair means,
resorted to a plan which the gambler undoubtedly thought
foul. Having gained the consent of the engineer to use the
engine, they concocted a plan rather bordering on that code
of laws generally known as coming under the especial
jurisdiction of Judge Lynch. They in the first place made
one end of a rope fast to the neck of the wondering
gambler, while the other was tied to the end of the piston
rod, allowing him two or three feet slack. They told him
that unless he shelled out their money instantly, they
would work the engine, and at the same time that they were
not responsible for any injuries he might sustain. Loth to
give up his gains, the fellow cast one look at the new
system of extortion, coolly calculated his chances, and
then told them they might ‘work away and be d—d.' No sooner
said than done, and the gambler was immediately seen
chasing the piston rod upon all fours, and then backing out
of its way. His eye all the time was as firmly set on the
rod as ever that of Herr Cline or Gabriel Ravel was upon
the tight rope. After working forward and backward several
times, one of his tormentors asked him: 'Don't you think it
best to hand over?' 'Don't bother me,' retorted the
gambler. 'You'll get sick of that fun,' said another of the
boatmen, as he was following the piston rod up in the
attitude of a bear. 'Not as you know on,' rejoined the
gambler as he backed out of the way. In this way they ran
upon the poor fellow for some time, he still manifesting an
unwillingness to give up his spoils. By this time all the
cabin passengers had heard of the fun going on below, and
went down to witness it. After a few moments' respite, the
engine again set in motion, and the gambler along with it.
The laugh from the bystanders boisterous and hearty in the
extreme, the poor fellow, intent upon nothing but his own
safety, followed the piston rod up to prevent his neck
being jerked off, and then backed out of its way to avoid
being fairly run over and crushed. We can liken his look
and actions to nothing old bear being dragged by chain up
to some point against his will, and backing out the moment
a foot of slack was given him; or else to a savage and
hungry bulldog, with a rope round his neck, fiercely
endeavoring to get at some prey, and then being dragged
back the moment his mouth was opened to secure it. 'Fire
and fall back,' was heard from an individual in the crowd.
'Root hog, or die,' came from another. 'Twig him—only
look,' says one. 'Here he goes, there he goes,' said a
second. 'Ha, ha, he, he, hi, hi, ho, no.' laughs another.
'Ain't he in pretty fix,' cried still a third. 'Serves him
right,' said a fourth. 'Good enough for him,' said a fifth,
the piston rod all the while keeping in full exercise, with
the perspiration rolling down his cheeks in streams. 'Ain't
you most ready to hand over now?' said one of the plucked
deck hands. 'Don't bother me,' say retorted the gambler,
'if you do, I'll lose my lick.' 'Won't you give up the
money!' said another of those he had fleeced. 'If do, do;
but if I do, I'll be D—D,' continued the companion of the
rod. ‘I've got the hang of this game—understand the
principles of this machinery now, and you may work me from
end of the Mississippi to the other, before I'll give up
the first red cent—that you may.' The gambler was worked in
this way until the boat was ready to start, without
flinching or showing any disposition to give up.
Considering that they had got the worth of their money out
of him in the shape of fun, and that he had worked hard and
afforded sufficient amusement to more than compensate for
their odd bits and picayunes, the engine was stopped and
the man let loose. After putting, blowing, and wiping the
perspiration from his face the gambler looked at his
tormentors with a self-satisfied air, and exclaimed, 'You
can't come it over this child with any of your common
games. I've stood three pluck one too often to be bluffed
off, even if there was

Article:
LYNCHING.-On the 16th inst, a mob of several hundred men
took from the jail of Williamstown (Ky.,) two persons Mays
and Cook, suspected of the murder of a drover named
Uuerback. They then erected a scaffold on the spot where
the crime was committed, called two priests to shrive the
prisoners and hanged them up according to the very letter
of lynch law. The affair was creating a great deal of
excitement in Kentucky. Recently in Illinois equally
summary punishment was inflicted on some gamblers who had
committed an atrocious murder. The rascals were pursued
several miles and when overtaken at least fifty bullets
were lodged in one of them. In the latter case, the
enormity of the crime and the reckless character of the
perpetrators, with the uncertainty of justice in that
portion of the country are stated as palliation of the
dreadful punishment inflicted.

them, the more we incline to approve any step calculated to
punish the, for such revolting outrage as they acknowledged
was by them committed. It appears that they went to the
house during his absence, and ordered his wife to give them
some liquor. On her refusing, they cursed her in
blasphemous terms and threatened her with violence if she
did not comply. After having gotten the liquor, they
demanded hot coffee and cold victuals, which they said she
would have to provide if she would not have her children
harmed, which they promised to do. After this, they
forcibly took from her an infant babe and rudely threw it
upon the floor, they threw her down, and while one
accomplished the fiendish designs of a rape, the other
pointed the muzzle of a loaded gun at her head and said he
would blow out her brains if she resisted or made the least
noise. They afterwards took the quilts and blankets from
the bed, broke open the trunks and drawers, and rifled
their contents, which consisted of forty dollars in specie
and a quantity of clothing, all of which they carefully put
up in the quilts and blankets. They even took the shoes
from off the feet of the woman and placing the whole of the
plunder on the back of a horse which they had brought with
them for the purpose, they made off. We obtained these
particulars from a gentleman of the highest responsibility.
He questioned the negroes on the subject a few hours prior
to their execution and also interrogated Mrs. Burnly in a
similar manner, and her answers agreed in every essential
particular with the statements made by the negroes. What
aggravates this affair is the fact that the unfortunate
woman had but six weeks previously recovered from
childbirth and her body is bruised and much hurt from the
rough treatment she received while in the hands of the
negroes, the prints of whose fingers were visible on her
neck. We have ever been, and now are, opposed to any kind
of punishment being administered under the statutes of
Judge Lynch, but when we reflect upon what must be the
feelings of the husband and father, and the deep anguish
which must invade the bosom of the injured wife and
outraged mother, due regard for candor and the preservation
of all that is held most sacred and all that is most dear
to man in the domestic circle of life, impels us to
acknowledge the fact that if the perpetrators of this
excessively revolting crime had been burnt alive, as was
first decreed, their fate would have been too good for such
diabolical and inhuman wretches.-Gallatin Signal, 11th
instant

Article:
Negro, a fiend, truly, who deserved the utmost severity of
the offended laws, was hurried from the county jail of this
county, and burnt at the stake - and not even a bill of
indictment was found by our grand jury against the
well-known participants in the act. Recently, a respited
criminal was taken from the jail of a neighboring county,
and executed by the populace - and we have heard of legal
proceedings against the leaders of the mob. In the counties
bordering on the western frontier, the lynching process,
for years has competed with the civil, almost to the
exclusion of the latter - a fact notorious in those
regions, and which the writer is prepared to prove. Last
winter, a stranger was shot in Buchanan County, in
endeavoring to escape from flogging, the penalty of a
suspicion of being connected with counterfeiters and no
investigation made of the matter. In Independence,
recently, it was declared by two of the most influential
citizens of that place, that had they been present when
certain of the participants in the Chavis affair were
arrested, those persons should have been immediately
executed - the writer has reason to believe it was no empty
declaration. As it was, they were maltreated by the mob;
men too, who have since been proven to have had little to
do with that transaction - while others were coerced to
make statements, under pain of death, which ultimately may
convict the innocent. These are facts which can be
sustained by irrefragable testimony - and it is but justice
when we are considering the causes which lead to the
aspersions of constitutional writers, that we should
consider them and utter against them our condemnation. To
pass them silently over, were to admit the validity of what
is not true - that they are the offspring of a form of
government which is the interest of the anti-republican to
vilify. Though lynch law is so common in this country, it
is by no means peculiar to it, a fact which our
calumniators seem entirely to overlook. In fact, there is
reason to believe that the very term is of European origin.
In a late work on Ireland (Thackeray's Irish Sketch Book,
p. 70) we are informed, in substance, that 'there is in
Deadman's Lane, Galway, "raw head and bones over door,"
commemorative of the following tragic affair. In 1493, the
Mayor of Galway, James Fitzstephen Lynch, came to the
knowledge of a murder committed by his son, some years
before at sea. Hereon, the culprit, was arraigned before
his own father, and sentenced to death. The clan Lynch,
however, rose in body to rescue the young man, and avert
such a disgrace from their family, but the father, another
Lucius Junius Brutus, frustrated their designs by hanging
his son with his own hands!' If this case did not give
origin to the phrase; it certainly deserved the
application. Alison himself admits and laments the frequent
occurrence of popular outbreaks in Europe - that even the
hero of Waterloo himself was 'reviled by majority of his
countrymen, execrated by the mob, narrowly escaping death
from their hands.' Yet, the existence of misrule in Europe
cannot apologize for its existence here. Recrimination can
effect but little of good in any case, as 'two wrongs can
never make a right.' Let then, being satisfied of the
necessity of the supremacy of law, to our ultimate
well-being as a nation, use every exertion to maintain that
supremacy, and abide the issue.

The Prophet and his Brother Hyrum Smith, Since our last the
official news has been received of the tragic deaths of Joe

MORE OF THE MORMONS The Mormons are to hold a Convention in
Baltimore on Saturday next. The original intention of the
Convention, as we are given to understand by the public
notice, was to nominate their late leader, Joe Smith, as a
candidate for the Presidency, but his death will render it
necessary to make other arrangements. The ST. Louis Era of
the 1st inst. has the following: The murder of Joe Smith
when in jail, after he had peaceably surrendered himself,
and after the solemn promise of the Governor that he should
be protected and have a fair trial, seems to meet with very
general condemnation. It is another flagrant instance of
the triumph of a mob spirit in the country. To murder
prisoners in cold blood when they are in custody and when
there is nothing to prevent their being punished to the
full extent of their crimes according to law, is utterly
inexcusable. But when mob raised and excited it knows no
bounds, no moderation, but reason and law are both
disregarded. We have often expressed the belief that mobs
and lynch law are improper under all circumstances, and
should not be justified, excused, or tolerated under any
circumstances, and every outbreak confirms the correctness
of this opinion. Joe Smith was under arrest, with public
sentiment strongly setting against him, there was the most
ample opportunity to convict and punish him legally and
severely. And in the St. Louis Democrat, we find the
following: From all the facts now before us, we regard
these homicides as nothing less than murder in cold
blood-murder against the plighted faith of the chief
magistrate of Illinois-murder of a character so atrocious
and so unjustifiable, as to leave the blacklist stain on
all its perpetrators-their aiders, abettors, and defenders.
Here was Joe Smith in the custody of the laws to which he
had surrendered himself, in the confidence that those laws
would not be broken to his injury. He had the promise of
preservation and protection against the very mob violence
to which he has fallen victim. Ought not such faith to have
been kept? Need we ask, indeed, whether, if there had been
special promise, the law does not always hold out implied
safety to its prisoners from all punishments, save what
itself imposes. Indeed the sight of such solemn pledges, so
shamefully broken, is truly sickening. Why, an Arab, if you
accept his hospitality, and eat of his salt-an American
Indian, if you once pass his threshold in peace, will give
up his existence before he will suffer his pledges to be
broken. If such acts are to be taken as a true expression
of the spirit which pervades the public mind of our
communities, it needs seer to tell us that our course as a
people is downward. It is a spirit which seeks its
qualification only in the indulgence of the most ignorant
prejudices and the vilest passions. Nothing can stand
against it, except the bayonets of despot and it's the very
spirit which, after a series of anarchies, naturally
produces despots and their bayonets. We think Smith
despicable impostor and that the dupes of deceit gross he
is must necessarily be most ignorant and debased. Hence we
have always thought that the laws of the land were strong
enough to control both him and them.

'Lynching in Panola.' Under the head of 'Lynching in
Panola,' the Memphis Enquirer of the 11th inst doubtless
through misinformation, makes a misstatement of facts. We
allude to the case of 'Ferguson,' lately arrested for
kidnapping the two little girls, and stealing negro from a
gentleman in Holmes county. The following paragraph
embodies the misstatement alluded to: 'After the two fiends
were taken they were handcuffed and brought back to Panola.
The citizens hearing the circumstances, and fearing that
they might in some way escape the punishment due their
crimes, organized themselves into an extra judicial
tribunal, and appointed a jury of twelve men, who sentenced
them to be severely cowhided, the sentence to be executed
the one upon the other. This was accordingly done, the
negro receiving thirty-five and the white man twenty-five
lashes well laid on with a cowhide. The sentence was for
each to receive fifty lashes, but they were so gashed with
the number above stated that the popular mercy rented the
balance. They were then handed over to their guard, to be
taken back to Holmes. Our informant heard in Panola that
the white man had been whipped to death by the citizens of
that county, but is not certain that his information is
correct. The informant of the Enquirer cannot be certain
that any of his 'information is correct.' The true
statement, as we derive it from those who were present, is
this. Ferguson and the negro were brought to this place
without handcuffs. Previous to their arrival, they had
evinced refractory disposition, on account of which they
were handcuffed together when they arrived here. During the
process of handcuffing Ferguson manifested a refractory
disposition, and among other things made threat, saying
gentlemen 'I will see you some other time' etc. This
produced an irritable state of feeling among the gentlemen
who had captured and had him in charge, and, in order to a
safe and convenient conveyance of the prisoner to Holmes
county, they thought it advisable that his and the negro's
refractory spirit should be first subdued by flagellation.
Accordingly they submitted to the citizens to say, not
whether the prisoners should be whipped, for that they had
already resolved on; but how much and how they should be
whipped. Such citizens as happened to be present (call it
jury or what you will) decided that the prisoners should
whip each other, fifty lashes each; provided the effect of
such whipping should not be in any manner to disable them
from travelling. This sentence was only in part executed,
the negro whipping so hard that it was thought prudent to
stop him. The enormity of the crime perpetrated jointly by
the white man and negro was such doubtless as to produce
strong feeling, but it did not manifest itself on the part
of the citizens of this place in the irrational excitement
which usually attends lynching operations. If it be
regarded as a case of lynching, the gentlemen who guarded
the prisoners,

Article:
The following sketch of Captain Rynders' life we have
obtained from various authentic sources. It will be seen by
it, that in him are found the elements which admirably
qualify him for popular leader of the Don Giovanni school,
bold, reckless and fearless with more wit than wisdom and
more promptitude than prudence--ambitious of being a
popular hero devoted to women, wine, and free living--fond
of fun and fight and always ready to protect the women and
the weak and defend the right against all odds. He was born
in the village of Waterford, Saratoga County, New York,
some thirty-eight winters ago. From the age of ten to the
year 1832 Mr. Rynders operated upon the North River, first
as hand, then as commander, when he got the title of
captain, and lastly as owner of two vessels. During this
period he sailed on several foreign voyages, to different
parts of the world. In these voyages occurred many exciting
incidents and thrilling adventures, which we have no room
to relate. In 30, the year of the cholera while in the
ownership and command of vessels upon the North River,
Captain Rynders, through sundry bad debts and speculations
upon the turf, to which he has always been slightly
addicted, failed, as many distinguished individuals have
done before and since. Unsuccessful in settling up his
debts, and his creditors being inexorable, in Dec. 1832,
Capt. Rynders sailed for New Orleans. As a specimen of
incidents which chequered his life upon the ocean we may
relate one or two adventures upon this passage to New
Orleans, as given to us by a passenger and eyewitness. The
captain of the packet was taken sick, and the whole duty
devolved upon the mate. The crew became refractory,
disobedient, and mutinous. Capt. Rynders saw the peril of
the ship, and, at the risk of his life, took side with the
mate, seized the helm, and by his boldness and decision,
Red Rover-like quelled the mutiny, and restored order. By
this coup de main, Capt Rynders saved the ship from the
rocks, when she was fast driving, having been steered upon
the wrong course, and all on board from shipwreck. The ship
was afterwards chased by pirates, to the great horror and
alarm of all on board, except our Don Giovanni. He resolved
on flight, and to that end called all hands to quarters;
mustered all the old swords, muskets, handspikes and
implements of fight which could be found on board, and
desperately resolved to repel boarders or die in the
attempt. The pirate came alongside but on discovering the
uncivil reception which they were likely to meet with, they
very wisely concluded to keep out of mischief and hauled
off. The commander of the vessel returned public thanks to
Captain Rynders, restored to him his passage money, and
expressed his lasting obligations to him for twice saving
his ship. Within three weeks after his arrival in New
Orleans, Captain Rynders became the hero of a popular row
in front of the Camp Street Theatre. These were the days
when the notorious pugilist O'Rourke was in his glory. On
the evening in question, O'Rourke was to have a boxing
match with a celebrated Englishman upon the boards of the
theatre. The theatre was jammed inside and thousands were
collected in front of it, chiefly Irish, and friends of
O'Rourke. In the excitement report reached the crowd
outside that O'Rourke was getting whipped by the
Englishman. The Irish were roused to frenzy, and resolved
on tearing down the theatre. And now was the crisis when
Captain Rynders stepped forth and contradicted the report,
told them the truth, and in short tickled the mob that they
actually bore him off in their arms in triumph. The next
adventure of the Captain was with O'Rourke himself, on
board the cabin of a steamboat. O'Rourke had lost money to
a gentleman at faro, got angry, and attempted to take his
life. At that time Captain Rynders knew nothing of the
game, but was assured by others that O'Rourke was in the
wrong, and that his money had been fairly won. This was
enough for Captain Rynders. He seized a red-hot poker, and
actually drove the pugilist out of the cabin. O’Rourke
afterwards acknowledged his error and became the fast
friend of Rynders. Severely afflicted with sickness at New
Orleans, and unsuccessful in obtaining business, in about
six months after his arrival there, Captain Rynders again
returned to New York, for the holy purpose, which for
twenty years he has steadily fulfilled, of taking care of
his aged parents. Again returning to New Orleans, his life
was little else than a series of personal encounters and
adventures, mainly on other persons' account. On one
occasion at a masquerade ball, a fight arose between a
couple of Virginians and several Frenchmen, with whom the
majority present appeared to take part. Obeying the
impulses of his nature, Captain Rynders took up for the
Virginians, who seemed ready and willing to fight, and at
it they went. Bowie knives were drawn, and used; pistols
were fired, and the fight became furious. In the melee
Captain Rynders received several severe cuts upon the back
of his neck and elsewhere, the marks of which he will carry
to his grave. A pistol was fired at his head, the ball
passing through his hat, and slightly grazing the left side
of his head. We next find our Captain in the Calaboose, for
whipping a couple of gens d’armes, who had attacked an old
man at the theatre. Not then understanding their true
character as policemen, Captain Rynders mistook them for
common soldiers, who had no rights above common citizens.
In this fight, after receiving more wounds and scars, he
whipped the gens d’armes, who went away, and returned with
the whole guard of twelve. To this guard, as he understood
their character, Captain Rynders surrendered with the
honors of war. As soon as explanation was made for the
charge, Captain Rynders was let go. At New Orleans, his
pockets were always open to strangers in necessity, from
the North. Many can attest to his liberality, while few can
remember that they have ever repaid it. One gentleman will
certainly remember that he forgot to hand over to Captain
Rynders' mother several hundred dollars, which he had
despatched by him to her. At Natchez, Capt. Rynders figured
extensively and always as a leader of every circle in which
he chanced to be, whether in bar room or ballroom, at the
theatre or the course, at meetings religious or political.
On one occasion a young man, a stranger to him, was, for
some cause, believed to be unjustifiable, seized by the
mob, who had resolved on summarily lynching him. Capt.
Rynders promptly and enthusiastically resolved that they
should do no such thing. He immediately raised a small
party of fifteen or twenty friends, rushed in among the
lynchers, and with bowie knife in one hand and pistol in
the other, rescued the young man from his frightful
situation, and bore him off to safety. Upon the Mississippi
Captain Rynders was well known, and became almost as famous
for his exploits as Paul Jones in the Northern Seas. His
adventurous and hair-breadth escapes would fill a volume.
In female intercourse, and in all matters of love, Captain
Rynders has always eminently distinguished himself, and
thought, felt, said, done his share. But other matters of
this kind now engross the public attention, we shall pass
them over with brief allusion to an affair of honor, in
which a fair Helen was concerned, which occurred on his
passage, upon a certain occasion, up to Wheeling. A
gentleman had insulted the wife of one of the passengers on
board. Such circumstance could not transpire either without
the knowledge of Captain Rynders, or without his taking up
the quarrel. He did take it up in defense of the lady.
Challenge to mortal combat was the consequence. The Captain
was known to be a Yankee, and his opponent was no little
surprised at his prompt acceptance of his challenge. He
chose pistols--seconds were selected--the case became
serious to the principals while outsiders anticipated rich
sport and bets ran high that the Yankee would get shot. At
the instance of all the passengers the boat was stopped,
and the parties went ashore to fight.

OUTRAGE LINCOLN COUNTY. We know that the people of Lincoln
County in this state have been much excited for some months
past over the discovery of the existence of a band of
counterfeiters and horse thieves among them. Several of
them have been at different times arrested, and suspicion
continued to rest against other families. In this state of
tension, a company of Regulators was formed to order the
suspected individuals to leave the county, failing to do
which, summary punishment was inflicted. Two young men of
the family named Turnbull fell under the suspicion of the
Regulators and on Friday last were met at a house in the
county to determine what should be done with them. It is
not known what was agreed upon at that meeting, but from
thence they proceeded to the residence of old Mr. Turnbull,
father of the young men in question. The old man, who was
at his shop, saw them approach and attempted to escape into
the house but was intercepted and caught. Two younger and
the females of the family retreated into the house and
locked the doors. The suspected men were not to be found.
The Lynchers surrounded the house for a time and finally
set fire to it, but it was extinguished by the family. They
then resolved upon more efficient measures and one of them
seized a tool with which, after several blows, broke the
door, and the mob entered. A general fight ensued. It is
not known which party fired first, but two shots were fired
by the young Turner, one of which killed a young man by the
name of Davis. He died only twenty-four hours after the
affray. Another of the mob, named Norrell or Norris, had
been injured in the fracas, having received a wound in the
head with a weapon resembling a corn knife, which
penetrated into the skull and he is not expected to live
long. A third was injured slightly. One of the Turnbulls
was shot in the knee and was dying at the last accounts.
The other was hit in the thigh and was not expected to
survive. One young boy, about sixteen years old, was
missing and unaccounted for. This occurred about eight
miles back of Baileyville between 11 and 12 o'clock of the
day. Great excitement followed throughout the county. The
mob had determined on meeting on Monday to proceed to the
Turnbull's house to exterminate the whole family, but it is
hoped that the efforts being made to arrest this design
will be successful. It is said that the Regulators are
composed of some of the respectable citizens of the county,
but how they can reconcile their proceedings with a desire
to maintain this character is beyond our comprehension. St.
Louis Republican.

Gazette gives an account of the apprehension of a man of
the name of Avant, and one of his confederates named
Powers, near Apalachicola. They were subsequently, taken to
Marianna in Jackson County, where they were hanged on
Friday, the 20th inst, without the form of trial, and
notice was at the same time given to four gentlemen of the
blackleg order, that if they were found in the place after
the lapse of ten hours, they should share the same fate. If
anything can palliate the atrocity of Lynch law, the
circumstances connected with one of these wretches would
almost justify this mode of punishment. Avant, a monster in
human form, and his life, for series of years, had been
marked by crimes of the deepest dye. He went to Pensacola
some years ago, a fugitive from justice from the State of
Alabama, where he had murdered a Sheriff. He had not been
long in Florida before he attempted the assassination of a
citizen, and being obliged to fly, proceeded to Marianna,
where he was concerned in the murder of another officer. He
then fled to the swamps contiguous to that town, where, up
to the time of his apprehension, and at the head of a band
of outlaws, he perpetrated murder and robbery upon all who
fell in his way. To such length, says the Gazette, had his
audacity been carried, it was considered dangerous to
travel through that part of the State. The peace and
well-being of the community demanded that such villains
should meet with retribution for his outrages, and owing to
the inefficiency of our Territorial government, jails have
been provided for the security of criminals; he and his
accomplice therefore, in order to ensure their punishment,
were brought to a speedy execution. Those concerned were
actuated by another motive; there are still remaining a
number of men of the same desperate character in the swamps
about the county and an example which the slow process of
law could not afford was necessary to strike them with
terror. The only sentiment which we can express on the
subject is regret that?

It was in the fall of '49. During the preceding summer, a
couple of slaves had been seduced and finally wrested from

southerners then at the north, filled with violent

abolition agents; sort of vindictive frenzy spread among

Two of the five murderers of Col. Davenport, William T.

mistaken, as the little child had the courage and presence

Thompson's Bank Note Reporter, of March 4th, warns the
public of new and dangerous counterfeit! As faithful
chroniclers of important events, we copy it, as follows: An
admirable Counterfeit One fine sunny day last week, we met
Plumbe in Broadway Plumbe, the unrivaled Daguerreotype
Professor. 'Come, Thompson, walk into my gallery,' says
Plumbe, 'I want to show you good counterfeit.' We walked in
'sit down,' says he 'head a little up and to the left fix
the eyes on that jackknife for one minute;' we did so 'all
is done,' says he, and disappeared through a door. In five
minutes he returned, with the best daguerreotype
counterfeit of his imagination. 'Zounds,' says we, 'that
might be passed on our wife for the genuine; you are a
dangerous man, sir, we shall lose our identity, if you can
make Thompsons in this manner what will become of
shinplaster banks and bankers;' he laughed, and we left.
Today, a friend informs us, we are exhibited in Plumbe's
Gallery, 251 Broadway, by the side of Jackson, Tyler, Polk,
Calhoun, Webster, Clay, and Cass. If any of our friends
from the North, South, East, or West are detained from home
longer than they expected, they should step into Plumbe's
and have a facsimile taken to send to their wives as

named Oliver Norris, was compelled, on account of
suspicions of misconduct, to leave Russellville, Illinois.
He was afterwards taken back, tried, and acquitted. He then
went to York, Illinois, where he remained till recently;
when, a horse being stolen and a friend of his disappearing
at the same time, he was suspected of being accessory to
the crime. He was consequently seized, flogged, and ducked
in the Wabash, the lynchers offered to release him if he
would name his accomplices. He named some of the most
respectable citizens of the county, among whom were John G.
Long and R. G. Wade. After his release, he returned with
his wife to Russellville, where he readily admitted that he
had slandered Long and Wade, alleging in his own
justification, that he had been compelled to give names,
and that the persons named by him were his enemies. Wade on
hearing this, swore that Norris should leave Russellville
immediately Norris' wife being in delicate health, and the
weather inclement, some of the citizens remonstrated with
Wade, proposing to let Norris remain for a short time and
then send him off quietly. Thereupon Wade became still more
exasperated, and taking Long with him went to Russellville,
hitched his horse in the street, and swore he would kill
Norris at sight. Some of the citizens gave Norris money to
bear his expenses, and advised him to depart immediately,
which he was about to do, when he met in the street Long
and Wade. They ordered him to give up his weapons, which he
readily did, handing his pistol to Wade. Long then examined
the condition of his own pistol, and tried the lock
deliberately. Norris, after giving up his pistol, raised
his hands in the most suppliant manner, walked backwards
and begged for his life on any condition. Wade first drew
club, then ran forward and struck Norris with his fist,
which turned him round facing Long, who, cocking his
pistol, took deliberate aim, and shot him through the head.
He fell and expired in about an hour after. Long and Wade
both left, and at the last dates had not been heard of.

RUM. A Coroner's inquest was held yesterday, on the body of
a beautiful boy, two years of age, killed by its own
father. It appears from the testimony that the father,

Dillon and had been thrown out of it by three men. He went

swearing vengeance against the three men. When home, he
loaded his gun, and placed the muzzle on the bed, cocked

contents passing through the head of the child. Cleveland

LYNCH LAW IN ARKANSAS. The overseer of Col. Walworth, rich
planter of Chicot County, Ark was murdered about a year
ago, by one of his slaves, who was tried and convicted of
the offense, but subsequently obtained a new trial. The
populace, fearing he would thus escape punishment, took the
law into their own hands, and on the 4th inst. mob repaired
to the jail cut down the door, notwithstanding the
remonstrance and resistance of the sheriff, entered the
prison and forcibly took the prisoner, led him forth with
halter round his neck, and in cold blood hung him to a tree
within 100 yards of the jail. GAMBLING. Green, the reformed
gambler, is lecturing at Wheeling.

A SERIOUS AFFAIR.--We are informed that, on Sunday evening
last, in Illinoistown, opposite this city, two men, coopers
by trade, in a drunken frolic, went in a house where they
insulted some ladies. One of the men was named John Hamer,
a German, and the other John Ray, an Englishman. The owner
of the house soon returned, and finding what had been done,
commenced an assault upon them, and beat them severely with
a hoop pole. The two fled to their boarding house.
Subsequently, a number of persons assembled and went to the
tavern where Hamer and Ray were in bed, took them out, and
after severely lynching them, put them into a skiff and
sent them over to this city. It is said that the skiff was
bored full of holes, and that they only gave them a couple
of sticks to work their way over on this side. The
Irishman, Ray, having made the most resistance, was worse
beaten than Hamer. They succeeded in reaching this side,
and since then, Ray has died of the injuries received.
Yesterday Hamer was taken to Belleville, to institute
proceedings against the parties engaged in the mob. Ray is
represented as a man of considerable property here, in
Peoria, and in Cincinnati, Ohio. In the latter place, he is
said to have a family. A considerable sum in gold, and a
number of deeds and other papers, left by him, are in the
possession of the keeper of the hotel in Illinoistown,
where he was staying. The subject, we are assured, will
undergo medical investigation. St. Louis Republican

Article:
From the Baltimore American. The following letter, from a
first-rate commercial source, will be read with interest:
SAN Francisco Dec. 9, 1848. We have little to note, since
my last, of a change in prices. The only article materially
affected is flour. Several cargoes from Chile and Oregon
have come in, and the last sales were at $4 instead of $50,
as my last reported. The other quotations are as before
stated. Liquors of all kinds keep up; ale and porter have
advanced, and sold at auction at $3 per dozen. Lumber has
advanced from 600 to $700 per square foot and will rise
higher as the demand is great to build houses for emigrants
pouring in from all parts where the information has reached
the richness of the gold region. I suppose you are all
convinced by the arrival of large sums in dust in the
United States and glad that the reports are to be relied
on. When the next steamer arrives, with $100,000 in dust
all further doubts will be at an end. The rainy season has
commenced, and the snows on the California Ridge will
interrupt the diggings to a considerable extent for two or
three months, when the miners will go at it again with
increased fervor. All the foreign population in the
neighboring islands are coming, and many of the natives and
although the number of houses erected and erecting are
numerous, so many persons come in every vessel that they
cannot find places to sleep. For small rooms not more than
70 feet square $90 per month in coin is the current rate. I
think the emigration will be so great from all parts of the
world, that their wants will keep prices up, and unless
shipments are very large no material change will take place
for a year or two in articles of necessity and of fancy,
because with the accumulation of wealth rapidly acquired,
people become extravagant and spend their money freely.
From what I have stated in this and former letters you can
draw your own conclusions and act accordingly. American
vessels are much wanted increased coast and freights are
high, seamen's wages $50 to $81 per month and American
laborers receive their $0 to $2 per day in coin, carpenters
$10. The United States cannot too soon send out strong
government to keep the loose population in order. Murders
are becoming rather frequent at the mines. A family of
eight, murdered a few days ago, and the persons who
committed the act, five runaway sailors or volunteers, were
lynched by hanging a few hours after. The population of
this place is orderly except when a large party comes in
from the mines with plenty of gold, and even then they
conduct themselves as well as could be expected. Commodore
Jones is here in the Ohio, in company with the Mary. He
will remain from two to three months but will keep the
ships cruising. The Ohio is ordered to Mazatlan suddenly to
keep the men from deserting, having already lost one
hundred men. When the steamers commence running it will
keep you well advised. The National Intelligencer of the
22nd has the following PANAMA, January 8, 1849. I have seen
several letters from San Francisco and one from a person at
the gold diggings who stated that a few loads of earth from
the dry diggings yielded, after washing, $16.90. Instances
are known where men have carried the earth to a place where
they could wash it, and have collected $500 and $1500 in a
day. These may be travelers' stories but Mr. Phelps who
left there in December says there is no romance attached to

were averaging from $50 to $100 per day, but the majority

ELLSWORTH.-The Lafayette (Ind.) Journal has the following
in regard to Charge Stockholm. We have been shown a private
letter from Mr. Ellsworth, dated at Stockholm Oct 30, 1848,
from which we are permitted to make an extract that would
seem to exculpate him entirely, and place upon another the
reproach with which he stands accused. The extract is
substantially in these words: He says Mr. T., alluding to a
gentleman whose name I purposely withheld had the impudence
to forward all the purchases he made during his journey to
my address and to expect that I would receive same free of
duty. Such collection never got together before:
serpentine, silk curtains, pewter, new linen, maps and
go-cart for children, carpets, hams, flour, and perfumery
contained in about twenty trunks and boxes. My refusal to
aid him, as he had expected, aroused his avarice, and led
him to employ ungentlemanly language in a note he wrote to
me. My answer was conceived and expressed with more feeling
than his own, and admitted of reply. As soon as I received
his communication, simply answered it as follows: My
morning has received all the consideration it eminently
deserves. Am, &c. W. ELLSWORTH. These few words threw him
into a most violent passion and he is welcome to continue
it to his pleasure. My whole action in the matter is right,
and I have therefore determined to stand without any
attempt at reconciliation. It is in fact a good finale to
the series of disagreeable interviews I have had with him
too much for petty quarrels, which, considering the person
who offended me are hardly worth sending.

We follow the Cairo Delta of the day, the following account
of lynching scrape in Hickman, NJ which illustrates fully
the evil effects of people in community of laws taking the
law into their own hands. It should be a lesson to those
who forget their allegiance to the regulations which
protect their lives and property. Several weeks since a
gentleman in Hickman had over three thousand dollars stolen
from him. Just when he was on the point of visiting a
distant place the money had been placed, we believe, in a
carpet bag, and that deposited for brief time in a box
under his counter of his store and covered with rubbish it
was stolen and a man living in the same house was
suspected. On this suspicion he was decoyed by his bosom
friend James Douglass. A band of enraged persons seized and
assaulted him and took him across the river. The victim
Wiley Brinkley, who was of a respectable family and a man
of bad character, was tortured by one hundred and fifty
lashes on his bare back to get from him on the old
inquisition principle confession that he stole the money.
His family was respectfully connected and respected among
these people and on mere suspicion publicly tortured to
wring confession of guilt whether guilty or not. Horrifying
to think or is disgraceful to the town whose citizens were
engaged in the affair and most disgraceful to those
citizens themselves. He did not confess. Brinkley kept his
bed several days after his punishment. He finally recovered
and as soon as he could proceeded into the street with
loaded double barreled gun. Mr. Douglass who believed was
highly esteemed shot him. Mr. Douglass was the first of the
band he met though others had accompanied them across the
river. Douglass fired one barrel, the load taking effect in
the mail of Douglass which was thrown across the lower part
of the deceased's breast. The second shot, however, missed.
Douglass fell down and died. The murderer told those
surrounding him that there were five lynchers yet. Another
murder came very near closing the scene or rather
continuing the acts. Brinkley surrendered himself to the
officers of justice defending his actions. We understand
that the citizens are in a state of great excitement, all
divided in their sides of approval or condemnation.

LYNCHING. We learn from the Boonville Observer, that
information got abroad in that city, that Mr. R. L.
Townsley had held his wife, while Mr. W. G. P. Townsley,
his brother, had severely whipped her with cowhide. Some of
the citizens drubbed one of the Townsleys, lynched and
ducked the other, for which they were tried, committed to
jail, and released on a writ of habeas corpus. The wife
testified that she had not been whipped. Glasgow Times.

There appears to have lately been some very serious
disturbances of the peace in the neighborhood of Metropolis
City, Illinois. One account says: There is a band of men
back of Metropolis, composed as we learn of the worst
characters, who set at defiance law and order, and are
known by the name of Flatheads. A body of citizens,
composed of good men, but of course having in their midst
evil characters, are called Regulators, and have been
formed to carry out the law. Some of the Flatheads stole
horses, and one of the Regulators who informed on them, was
caught, lynched and tied naked to a tree during night,
exposed to the mosquitoes and weather. He died several days
thereafter, but before his death he gave the names of
several persons he had recognized. The Sheriff found them,
but they refused to deliver themselves up unless they could
be tried by Magistrates of their own selections, who of
course would screen them. The Sheriff could not do this,
and they were not arrested at the time. The Flatheads
gathered to the number of about two hundred. The Regulators
assembled, and there was prospect of battle last week. The
Flatheads finally secured and fortified themselves in a
large log house, about twelve miles back of Metropolis, to
the number of about one hundred and sixty, with two cannons
and ammunition. The Regulators were rallying last Friday
(27th ult.), and had sent to Paducah and Smithland for
cannon, with the determination to arrest the three men. A
grand fight was expected to come off last Saturday (28th
ult). Another story given by Dr. Young to the editor of the
Cairo Delta, is as follows: Two or three weeks ago a barn
belonging to Mr. Tolson, was set on fire and burned down.
Mr. Tolson and Mr. Shell, who are brothers-in-law, stand in
the position of leaders-the first of the Flatheads, and the
second of the Regulators and both are men of influence. The
incendiary was traced to the house of a Regulator named
Douglass, who, with a young man of bad character named
Bruce, confessed to setting fire to the barn, but turned
State's evidence, and said they had been employed by
certain Regulators to murder prominent citizens of
Metropolis. Things now began to grow exciting. Backus was
whipped by 'the Lynns,' a family of very bad reputation
belonging to the Flathead side, who were once driven from
Kentucky for misconduct, and who were prominent in these
difficulties. Arrests were made on both sides by
constables, and affairs were approaching a bloody crisis,
when Dr. Young, who says he had been occupying neutral
position, was chosen as peace-maker by the Flatheads, and
in this capacity went to the opposite party. He made speech
to the Regulators, and gave them such assurance of peace
from the other party, and of their limited force and
preparations, that the constable dismissed the band,
numbering about one hundred and fifty. A guard of six
Regulators started out with Dr. Y. to escort him back. This
was on Saturday morning last the 28th ult. When about seven
miles from Metropolis, they arrived in sight of the
Flatheads, who numbered sixty. Here doctor took our
informant aside, and urged him to fly, as there were
hundred Regulators in ambush close by. While they were
talking, the Regulators rushed out and attacked the other
party. Dr. Y. ran up to make peace, but fell stunned by a
ball, which passed through his hat and grazed his head. The
Flatheads fled, the Lynn family having been the first to
set the example. Two of the Flathead band, Samuel Taylor
and Robt. Canada were killed, and another wounded, Daniel
Enlow, son of Col. Enlow, formerly Representative from
Massac County. On the side of the Regulators, a man named
Clinton King, who had been the cause of much of the strife,
was killed, and two others wounded, one dangerously. The
sheriff, Read, had gone home when he thought peace for the
time was established. Both parties were all armed. Dr.
Young went to Metropolis, but was warned to fly as the
Regulators wished to take his life, and was provided with
means. He was here on Tuesday, and says he is going to see
the Governor, and lay the state of things before him. He
describes affairs in Massac County as ruinous and growing
worse daily. He says there are good men in both parties,
but the mass are ruffians and loafers. Ocean navigation
through the St. Lawrence River still interdicted.- Several

Article:
Execution of All, the murderer of Mr. Anderson, at that
place, on the 20th ult. The murder of Mr. A. was one of the
most atrocious and cold-blooded deeds that we have ever
been called on to record, and it demanded, in the strongest
terms, the severest penalty of the offended law. But did
the enormity of his crime justify a departure from the due
course of law and a resort to Lynch law? We think not; and
we are sorry to see such manifestations of the popular
will, in any case, especially where the laws of our country
have provided an adequate and proper punishment. The
presses of other states have always taken peculiar delight
in harping upon the morals of our people, and we fear that
the recent occurrence at Bentonville will be caught up as
another instance of the laxity of morals in Arkansas. We
sincerely hope this may be the last manifestation of Lynch
law in the state. Bentonville, August 21st, 1849. Dear
Clarke: Under the impression that you are anxious to know
the result and finale of Alife, the murderer of Anderson, I
make haste to detail what took place yesterday before his
execution. Early in the morning, the people began crowding
in until it swelled to a great multitude, such as perhaps
never assembled there before. There seemed to be various
opinions as to the proper course to pursue. Some were for
delivering him for trial and execution, and some for
summary punishment. The near relatives of the deceased were
consulted, who said they delivered him up to the people to
do with him as they pleased. Finally, 11 o'clock came, and
there was no movement towards any definite course—still
there was no excitement amongst the multitude. About this
time, the Sheriff and Major Howard appeared at the court
house steps, when the Sheriff called upon the people to
draw near. Major Howard addressed them. He commended them
for their goodness, and said that it was a fair indication
that whatever they did would be most apt to be right. He
then condemned, in the strongest terms, all mobs and the
principles of mobocracy. At this juncture, his numerous
friends began to suspect that he would oppose any action of
a summary character, for they well knew his violent
opposition to all grades of mobs. He then recounted the
history of the present case—the prisoner's open confession,
never attempting to deny doing the deed, and in all his
confessions suggesting no cause of defense, nor did any
person for him, and that it was the prisoner's own wish to
be hung here, and not carried to your county; therefore,
his execution here in summary manner would not be
characterized by any act or spirit of mobocracy. Why try
him? There was no defense which he wished to make, and it
was mockery of common sense to go through the forms of law,
merely for form's sake. He then requested those in favor of
hanging him to move to the right, and those in favor of
sending him to Crawford to the left. Every person moved to
the right. He then requested those in favor of erecting a
temporary gallows and hanging him at 1 o'clock to move to
the left, all went. He said he had told lies about the
manner of killing his master and wished to explain under
the gallows. Here follows his confession as to the manner
of killing his master, which we noticed last week. He was
hung and buried. A more hardened, daring demon never died.
Yours, in haste, etc. We received a letter from Bentonville
on Thursday, in which we desired to say that the negro did
not accuse the white man of 'instigating him to commit the
murder, but that he had been brought to it by associating
with the white man. The writer further says that some
persons were afraid to risk the negro in the Van Buren Jail
for six or perhaps twelve months. The opinion we have given
above on the subject remains unaltered, and we again say,
we hope that it may be the last instance of Lynch law we
may be called on to record.

ALL THE HONESTY AND COURAGE. We give below from the Natchez
Free Trader, another specimen of Taylor's appointments. The

Whig! THAT covers a multitude of sins. The PLANK ROADS. The
planking of the Detroit and Howell road is rapidly
progressing. Already the plank is down several miles and
gate erected. This road is one of the greatest
thoroughfares in the State and will be made still greater
by the planking of it. It will enable farmers to get into
market at all of the year, with double the loads that they
have heretofore been able to draw. The Detroit and
Birmingham plank road is also rapidly progressing. One mile
of the plank is already down, and the work of grading and
placing plank on the line is going forward rapidly. This is
the thoroughfare in the State. Even in these dull times
teams are continually passing to and from the city over the
road. The city is destined to reap a rich harvest by means
of these roads. Plank roads make business. Every good
farmer keeps a team, and with good roads and low toll at
all seasons, a vast amount of produce, wood, etc., will be
brought to market by those who have not been able to do so
heretofore. This will create greater competition in the
market, and enable all to purchase the necessaries much
cheaper. At the same time, the profits of the producer will
be increased from the fact that larger loads be drawn and
teams turned to better account. We hope to see the charters
granted in 1848 in various parts of the State, taken, and
the work commenced. The charters of the Detroit and Saline
the Detroit and Utica, the Detroit and Erin, the Jackson
and Lansing, etc., are all good, and the several routes lay
through the best parts of the State. The stock will not
only be good, but the increased facilities to farmers will
tend to open and settle the unoccupied lands. Every farmer
who has any spare means should be a stockholder in the road
which is nearest to his farm. Detroit Free Press NORWEGIAN
WATER TELESCOPES An instrument which the people of Norway
have found of so great utility that there is scarcely a
single fishing boat without one is the water telescope or
tube, of three or four feet in length, which they carry in
their boats with them when they go fishing. When they reach
the fishing grounds, they immerse one end of this telescope
in the water, and look through the tube. Objects deep are
seen distinctly as if they were within a few feet of the
surface; by which means, when a shoal of fish comes into
their bays, the Norwegians instantly prepare their nets,
man their boats, and go out in pursuit. The first process
is minutely to survey the ground with their glasses, and
where they find the fish swarming about in great numbers
they give the signal and surround the fish with their large
draft nets, and often catch them in hundreds at a time.
Without these telescopes, their business would often prove
precarious and improbable, as the fish, by these glasses,
are distinctly seen in the deep clear sea of Norway, as
goldfish in a crystal jar. This instrument is not only used
by the fishermen but is also found in the navy and coasting
vessels of Norway. When their anchors get into foul ground
or their cables warped roadstead they immediately apply the
glass, and, guided by it, take steps to put all to rights,
which they could not do so easily without the aid of this
rude and simple instrument, which the meanest fisherman can
make up with his own hands without the aid of a craftsman.
This instrument has been lately adopted by the Scotch
fishermen on the bay, and by its assistance they have been
enabled to discover stones, holes and uneven ground, which
their nets travel and it has been found the telescope
answered to admiration, the object in twelve feet of water
being as clearly seen as the surface.

Lynching and Robbery in Tennessee.-The Memphis Enquirer, of
the 7th, says: Some few days since, an old man named Holt,
living at Moscow, in Fayette county, got drunk, when he was
enticed off by two young men, who took him to the swamp,
whipped him unmercifully, robbed him of about $70 and would
have killed him had it not been for the timely approach of
the citizens of Moscow, who were attracted by the cries of
the suffering old man. The young men took leg bail, but
were pursued by a number of citizens, and it is hoped they
will be arrested.

The steamship Falcon, 5 days and 18 hours from Chagres,
arrived at New Orleans on the 5th inst. having made it is

From the Alta California, published at San Francisco:
Population, streets present a busy and populous appearance.
In the business portion of town the highways are so
thronged with drays, wagons and people that it is sometimes
difficult to push way through the crowd. The population has
increased more than one hundred percent within the last
three months, and the new business establishments have
increased in still greater ratio. The Public Health: The
general health of the 5000 inhabitants of San Francisco
good. Recently some deaths have occurred from diarrhea and
dysentery, and many are now suffering from one or the other
of these diseases; but the sickness is abating. Some
solicitude is felt in regard to cholera and ship fever but
the general opinion is that neither of these diseases can
spread in such climate as this, although it is highly
probable that out of 10 cases would prove fatal. Hospitals:
Several large and well-arranged hospitals are now
established in the city, it is very gratifying to know that
