Index Number: preciv7

Article:
The text will be found in the Delaware Gazette of last
week, and is as follows: For the Delaware Gazette. Mr.
Editor, I see some comments in the Journal respecting the
lynching of the negro Hamilton, at Smyrna. He inclines to
extenuate the crime, and seems to think it was hatred
towards the negroes, that it was violation of law, so, etc.
Wonder what Kent would think if he caught a negro, or even
a white man violating his daughter. Would he not shoot or
hang him on the spot or even for the attempt? Is not the
attempt as great as the crime in his instance? We are, none
of us, I hope, in favor of mob law on a general scale, but
desperate cases require desperate means. He seems to have
great sympathy for the injured family, and yet greater
sympathy for the negro. I believe it is all perfectly
right, not because his skin is black for I could have hung
Kent just as soon as a negro. If we here are tinctured with
Negrophobia--probably he is strongly tinctured with Black
Republicanism. Citizen. Now this means simply to apologize
for mob.

Article:
MURDER. A dispatch to the Union states that a shocking
murder was committed near Fort Churchill last Monday night.
Wm. Goshart killed a man named McMullitt with a knife.
Goshart was arrested and taken to Carson City. He narrowly
escaped being lynched.

Index Number: preciv4

Article:
A REVOLUTIONARY SOLDIER LYNCHED. A Hatteras correspondent
of the New York Tribune says: 'a lady just from Wilmington,
North Carolina, tells me that when the news of the Federal
victory at Hatteras arrived there, a company of men were
assembled in a store and extolling the secession flag, when
an old revolutionary soldier (the only one known to be
living in North Carolina) interfered, and asked the
secessionists if they knew how much the Stars and Stripes
cost? He said he did, for he fought under them and saw them
when first raised, and that he would never recognize
another. At this, he was taken, his head half shaved,
plaster put on, and the plaster covered with tar, and the
tar with feathers, and then he was hurled into the street.'

Article:
WOULDN'T TELL LIE. - An incident was narrated recently, in
the Court of Sessions, illustrating the veracity of the
Celestials. A miner's cabin was broken into and seven
hundred dollars in coin and a watch stolen. Very strong
circumstances pointing to John, formerly in the employ of
the injured party, as the thief he was seized and sentenced
by Judge Lynch to be hanged till he confessed. Under the
sentence, John, protesting his innocence, was hauled some
dozen times over a stout limb, but the last ascension
proving too much for the Celestial's fortitude, he owned
up, and agreed to pilot his tormentors to the hidden booty,
and did so. While the miners were unearthing the ill-gotten
treasure, John looked on very plum, but when the last
'twenty' was exhumed, his countenance frightened, and
slapping the leader of the choking inquisition triumphantly
on the back, he exclaimed, 'You see, John, me no tell lie.'
COURT OF SESSIONS - The motion for a new trial in the case
of L. P. Huntsman, convicted of an assault to do bodily
harm, was argued on Saturday afternoon, and overruled. The
defendant was sentenced to pay fine of $50, or, in default
of payment, be imprisoned in the county jail for
seventy-five days. The second trial of John Vintage,
indicted for assault with intent to murder, was commenced
yesterday morning, and the day occupied in empaneling jury
and hearing testimony for the prosecution. The witnesses
for the defense gave their testimony this forenoon, and the
case is now being argued by counsel. DISTRICT COURT - In
the District Court, on Monday, the motion for new trial in
the case of the Eureka Lake Co. VS. Van Hagan, was
overruled. The motion for new trial in the case of McDaniel
VS. Stidger, was set for hearing on Monday next. Nichols et
al. VS. White - continued for one week. Wm. Brodie admitted
to citizenship. This afternoon, the Court appointed the
Sheriff assignee in the case of Samuel Oakes, an insolvent
debtor. In the case of the Eureka Lake Co. VS. Van Hagan,
the appeal bond was fixed at $4,000. CONNECTION WITH THE
AUBURN STAGE - The California Stage Company have commenced
running two-horse stage from Auburn to connect with the
Nevada stage running to Lincoln. The stage leaves Auburn at
ten o'clock every morning, and connects with the Nevada
stage six miles west of the former place. By this
arrangement, passengers from Nevada can go direct to
Auburn, if they so desire, instead of going to Lincoln. GAS
LIGHT - The Nevada Gas Co. put up yesterday, large street
lamp on their building, which is kept burning all night.
This is a decided improvement. It cheers the belated
pedestrians wending their way to Aristocracy Hill and its
reflection on the adjoining brick blocks gives that part of
our town a city look. It is particularly pleasing to those
who remember when our town was composed of log cabins and
shake shanties. THE HENNESS ROAD - Man's saddle train
arrived in town yesterday morning, direct from Virginia
City, by way of the Henness Pass. We learn from the driver
that good trail is now open for horsemen and pack animals.
HOSE NG. - Messrs. Terry & Irving, No. 81 Broad Street, are
busily employed in manufacturing hose for the miners. They
turn out about one hundred yards a day.
OBSERVATION-DISCLOSURES, appropriate for the occasion, will
be held by Rev. Mr. Briefly, at the Baptist Church, on
Thanksgiving day.

Headline: SeryiIe InsurrectIOns in South Carolina
Fearful Appehensions and Punishments.

LLM Explains: The article provides a firsthand account of events in
Charleston, including specific instances of retaliation
using lynch law against slaves involved in revolts, such as
burning them to death. The article contains vivid
descriptions of these punishments, which indicates it
describes specific lynching events that have already
happened.
Index Number: preciv2

Article:
From the Philadelphia Inquirer, 30th We are permitted to
copy the following letter, written to a lady in this city,
from a relative in Charleston, South Carolina. The
statements made therein may be relied upon as an accurate
description of affairs in that city at the present time.
CHARLESTON, S.C., Nov. %, 1861. Disguise the truth as we
may, all thinking men here feel their position peculiarly
unsafe and those who are surrounded by female relatives
have their anxiety increased thousandfold. We do not fear
for the clash of contending armies, though that is
sufficiently terrible to excite much apprehension; but even
amid the carnage of war, the veriest boors within the
armies would respect women though traitors try to teach us
that the northern war cry is beauty and booty: but we do
dread lest at midnight the fearful sounds of servile
insurrection shall salute our ears. You know the negroes
are far superior in number to the whites and now that so
many are absent in the army their majority is greatly
increased. If they rise we are in their power. Do you know
what that means? Remember the history of all servile
insurrections, and recall the horrors enacted by the race
whom oppression has helped to brutalize. Of course the
masters would fight of male whites defend their helpless
wives and daughters against a tenfold force of maddened
slaves, whose strength and ferocity are well known! No
general insurrection has taken place, though several
revolts have been attempted quite recently and in these
cases entire families were murdered before the rioters were
subdued. Then came retaliation of the most fearful
character. At any time where servants assail or murder
white persons, speedy and severe punishment is administered
but now they do not wait for the action of the law lynch
law prevails. In these revolts, which occurred in the
interior of the state, most of the servants who
participated were either shot in the conflict or as soon as
captured, and two of them were burned to death. To say they
were burned to death seems a simple sentence, devoid of any
special horror; but the scene as described to me by a
witness was too dreadful for mortal eyes. Imagine the poor
wretches, red with the blood of their masters, cowering in
the hands of those from whom they need not look for pity;
not even for time to repent of deeds which exclude them
from hope hereafter. They are dogged and defiant toward
their captors, until their doom is pronounced—a fate of
which they have a special horror. Dragged to the place of
execution, within sight of their own houses, surrounded by
their fellow servants, who are compelled to witness the
sight, they are bound to strong trees, with great heaps of
pine knots piled close around their persons. Directly the
torch is applied, and the inflammable pine bursts into a
vivid flame. When the blaze reaches the bodies, and the
sensitive flesh peels and crackles, their cries are too
fearful to be heard by human ears. Nor is the torment soon
over. The flames scorch the upper part of the bodies,
producing exquisite agony, but slowly burn into the vitals,
until the wretched sufferers go to Judgment with all their
crimes upon their heads. I undertook to say the
apprehension of servile insurrection lost its power when,
as time passed, all seemed peaceful, so we easily fell back
into dreams of security until these events aroused us to
watchfulness. This action is suppressed as far as possible,
and kept entirely from the papers, for the negroes hear
what is published, if they do not read it, and such
examples might produce disastrous consequences.

Index Number: preciv1

Article:
Trial of Richard Evans for the Murder of John Howard The
trial of Richard Evans, charged with the murder of John T.
Howard in this city, on the 10th day of May last, was
commenced yesterday. The deceased was three months
volunteer, and belonged to Capt. Nalley's company. Dr.
Helen sworn. Knew the deceased; was called on to attend him
at the Infirmary; found the deceased lying on the floor,
insensible, and in a dying condition; he died in about
twenty minutes after witness was at the post mortem
examination; Howard was shot over the left eyebrow, the
ball entering the brain; extracted the bullet from the head
of deceased. Witness ceased. Justice Thompson sworn.
Testified that Dr. Helen showed him the ball that he (Dr.
Helen) extracted from the head of deceased. Daniel Whalen
sworn. Knows the prisoner saw McCarty and Evans on the
corner of Sixth and Pennsylvania avenue, about five minutes
before the shooting occurred. Witness stopped and told
soldier, who inquired the time, that it wanted ten minutes
to nine. Heard the pistol go off; ran to the corner of
Brown's Hotel, and saw several men carrying deceased to
lamp post. Took a drink at Werner's; saw Evans hand Notary
something; don't know what it was; Evans came and stayed
with witness until 4 o'clock; was with Evans; went to
Marble Alley with him; there had been disturbance there.
Captain Goddard testified that the pistol was handed him by
Squire Thompson; witness tried to get the loads out, but
did not succeed. Charles McCarty sworn. Testified that he
did not know Howard; knows the prisoner was in Werner's
restaurant; saw the prisoner and his partner, Whalen, come
in, they did not stay long before they left. They had been
gone some two or three minutes before he heard report of a
pistol. Witness, in the act of drinking a glass of beer,
ran out and went to the people picking up deceased. The
crowd was halloaing, 'Lynch him!' 'Lynch him!' 'There he
goes!' 'There he goes!' Witness started down the street
when he met the prisoner, who was all atrimble. Witness
told the prisoner to hand him his pistol, or the crowd
would hang him on the spot, if he was found, upon
examination, to have it in his possession. Witness then
went over, and deposited it with a Mr. Cox, barkeeper for
Werner; they both went in to the cellar, and examined the
pistol, and thinks it looked as though it had just been
fired. Witness left the pistol with Cox, and came out; met
the prisoner on the corner; he was very much scared, saying
to witness, 'My life is in your hands,' or 'I am in your
hands,' or 'The whole matter is your hands!' witness cannot
remember which. Cross-examined. Did not arrest the
prisoner; the crowd did not disperse for some time after
Howard was shot; did not make any report to any officer
until next morning, when he told Mr. Phillips, the deputy
marshal. Saw Werner's and get drink; did not see them go
out exactly together; there may have been a few seconds
between; but they were both on, when witness heard the
report of a pistol. Witness then ran out saw people going
towards Brown's Hotel, have known the prisoner a year or
two; thinks he was one of the best men on the watch was
afraid the crowd would hang the prisoner; was very friendly
towards him. Met Whalen on The Gother; was on one side of
prisoner and Whalen on the other; the crowd was crying out,
'No. 32.' Witness knew that the prisoner's number was not.
Lewis Kease sworn. Knows the prisoner. Witness keeps cigar
store on the corner of Sixth street and Pennsylvania
avenue. Knew store door about half past eight O'Clock on
the 10th of May last; saw young man dressed in soldier's
clothes, running, policeman after him. He ran as far as
Sixth street. There was hack with two grey horses attached,
standing there. The deceased swung himself around the pole
of the hack, and came the pavement. The policeman that was
after him ran as far as the ladies' entrance of Brown's
Hotel. Witness saw the prisoner eight or ten yards from the
lamp post. The deceased turned, saw the prisoner standing
in the street, turned to run up Sixth street. Just as
deceased turned, witness saw the prisoner pull a pistol
from his immediately on his face, bruising his forehead
very much. The prisoner then turned and went in the
direction of Parker's store. Witness saw the prisoner put
his pistol back into his pocket. The lamps were burning,
and everything very quiet Has known the deceased for some
fifteen or sixteen months. The deceased belonged to Capt.
Nalley's company Metropolitan Rifles. The court then
adjourned until this morning.
